issue.issue_text: On the question whether s. 187-A violated Arl 14 of the Constitution on the grounds; (I) that tho Customs authorities had an absolute discretion to proceed either under s. 167(8) in which case there would be only an imposition of a fiscal penalty and confiscation of goods; or to fi!e a com-plaint in the criminal court under s. 187 A for the offence under s. 167 item 81, in which case there couJd also be a sentence of imprisonment up to two years.

facts: The appellant was prosecuted and convicted for importing contraband goods under s. 167, item 81, of the Sea Customs Act, 1878, following a complaint filed by a customs authority under s. 187-A.
The appellant challenged the constitutionality of s. 187-A, arguing it violated Article 14.

The argument was that the Act gave customs authorities an unguided and absolute discretion to either proceed with only a fiscal penalty and confiscation under s. 167(8) or to also initiate a criminal prosecution under s. 167(81), which could lead to imprisonment.
law: Public officials vested with discretionary power are required to act in a reasonable and bona fide manner, not according to their whim and fancy.
Procedural provisions of a law must be interpreted in light of the overall object and purpose of the Act.
The exercise of discretionary power by an authority is subject to judicial review and can be challenged in court if it is used arbitrarily or discriminatorily.
application: The Court held that the power granted to customs authorities under s. 187-A is not an unguided or absolute power.

The decision to file a criminal complaint is guided by specific criteria that the officer must consider. These include the "enormity and magnitude of the contravention" and the sufficiency of the "evidence which is available" for a criminal trial.
The Court reasoned that in some cases, evidence might be insufficient for a criminal prosecution, justifying the decision not to file a complaint.

It was established that customs officers are bound to examine the facts of each case and cannot discriminate between similar cases. If they do act arbitrarily, their decision can be challenged in appropriate legal proceedings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, holding that s. 187-A did not violate Article 14 because the discretion given to customs authorities to initiate criminal prosecution is not absolute or unguided. The decision must be based on reasonable criteria, such as the seriousness of the offense and the strength of the evidence, and is subject to judicial review to prevent arbitrary use.

issue.issue_text: On the question whether s. 187-A violated Arl 14 of the Constitution on the grounds; (2) the customs officials have a wide latitude in choosing cases for criminal prosecution,

facts: The appellant was prosecuted for an offence under s. 167, item 81, of the Sea Customs Act, 1878, following a complaint filed by a customs authority under s. 187-A.

Section 187-A requires that a complaint for such an offence be made by a high-ranking official, specifically the Chief Customs Officer or an officer not lower in rank than an Assistant Collector of Customs.
law: A law that confers discretionary power on an authority is not necessarily a violation of Article 14 of the Constitution if the power is not unguided or arbitrary.
The guidance for exercising such discretion can be found in the object, purpose, and overall scheme of the statute itself.
The exercise of discretionary power must be reasonable, bona fide, and not based on whim or fancy. If it is not, the exercise of that power can be challenged in appropriate proceedings.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the discretion given to customs officials under s. 187-A is not unguided.
The guidance comes from the object and purpose of the Sea Customs Act, which is to enforce customs duties and prohibitions on imports and exports.
In deciding whether to file a criminal complaint, an officer must consider relevant factors such as the 'enormity and magnitude of the contravention' and the 'evidence which is available'.
The Court noted that the power is vested in high-ranking, responsible officers, not minor officials, who are expected to act reasonably.

Drawing a parallel to the Industrial Disputes Act (as interpreted in the Niemla Textiles case), the Court found that the purpose of the Act itself controls the exercise of discretion, preventing it from being arbitrary.
Therefore, the officials cannot simply discriminate between similar cases according to their 'whim and fancy'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that s. 187-A does not confer an unguided or arbitrary power on customs officials. The discretion to prosecute is guided by the purpose and scheme of the Act and relevant factors of the case, and therefore, it does not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.

arguments.issue_text: On the question whether s. 187-A violated Arl 14 of the Constitution on the grounds; (I) that tho Customs authorities had an absolute discretion to proceed either under s. 167(8) in which case there would be only an imposition of a fiscal penalty and confiscation of goods; or to fi!e a com-plaint in the criminal court under s. 187 A for the offence under s. 167 item 81, in which case there couJd also be a sentence of imprisonment up to two years.
appellant_arguments: The offences could be dealt with by customs authorities under s. 167(8) (resulting in penalties) or by instituting a prosecution in a criminal court under s. 187A (resulting in imprisonment).
The option given to officers to file a complaint or not constitutes a clear infringement of Article 14.
This discretion leads to and has resulted in discrimination, as in some cases, no complaints were filed, and only proceedings under s. 167(8) were taken, resulting only in penalties.

This discretion has led to actual discrimination, where some individuals only faced penalties under s. 167(8) while others faced criminal prosecution.

cases.case_name: Nirmala Textiles Furnishing Mills Ltd. v. The Second Industrial Tribunal
cases.principle: It was cited for the principle that where the purpose, scope, and overall scheme of an Act are well-defined, they provide sufficient guidance to control the exercise of discretion conferred by the Act, thus preventing the power from being arbitrary or discriminatory in violation of Article 14.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a statute grants authorities the discretion to initiate criminal prosecution, that power is not arbitrary but is guided by the object, purpose, and scheme of the Act. The authorities must exercise this power reasonably, in good faith, and cannot discriminate between similar cases according to their whim and fancy.
obiter: Authorities are expected to take into account the changed conditions obtaining after the enforcement of the Constitution, which guarantees fundamental rights including Article 14, when deciding whether to launch a prosecution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The discretionary power granted to customs authorities under s. 187-A to either file a criminal complaint or proceed with departmental penalties is not unguided or arbitrary, and therefore does not violate Article 14 of the Constitution. This power must be exercised for effectuating the object and purpose of the Act, keeping in view its entire scheme. The authorities are bound to act in a reasonable and bona fide manner, taking into account factors like the enormity of the contravention and the sufficiency of evidence, and cannot discriminate between similar cases according to their whim and fancy.
legal_tests_applied: A discretionary power is not necessarily a discriminatory power, and abuse of power is not to be easily assumed where the discretion is vested in the government and not in a minor official.
Procedural provisions must be read in the light of the object and purpose of the Act, which can provide the necessary guidance to control the exercise of discretion.
The exercise of discretion can be challenged in appropriate proceedings if it is not exercised in a reasonable and bona fide manner.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the discretion was absolute, finding instead that it was guided by the object, purpose, and scheme of the Act, which is to ensure duties are levied and prohibitions are enforced.
The court specified the criteria that must guide the customs officer's decision, namely 'the enormity and magnitude of the contravention and the evidence which is available'.
The court held that the existence of discretion is not inherently unconstitutional, citing numerous other Acts where authorities have similar powers to grant or withhold sanction for prosecution.

The court affirmed that if the authorities abuse their discretion and 'discriminate between similar cases according to their whim and fancy,' it is 'always open to a person against whom complaint has been instituted to challenge their exercise of discretion in appropriate proceedings,' meaning the power is not unchecked.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the implicit argument that the discretion under s. 187-A is not unguided, but rather constrained by the overall purpose and scheme of the Act.

The court analogized the situation to the one in Niemla Textiles Finishing Mills Ltd. v. The 2nd Industrial Tribunal, where the purpose of the Industrial Disputes Act was found to be a sufficient guide for the government's discretion to refer disputes.
The court relied on the principle from Matajog Dobay v. H. C. Bhari that a discretionary power is not necessarily a discriminatory one, and its abuse cannot be presumed.

The court reasoned that officers must act in a 'reasonable and bona fide manner' and that a practical reason for discretion exists, such as when evidence is insufficient for a criminal court but sufficient for a departmental penalty.
policy_considerations: The court acknowledged that authorities are 'expected to take into account the changed conditions obtaining after the enforcement of our Constitution which guarantees fundamental rights including Art. 14.'

The court recognized the practical necessity for such discretion, stating, 'It is possible that in certain cases the evidence may not be sufficient for taking the matter to a criminal court and in view of the entire facts a complaint may not be lodged.'

The court noted that in many laws, provisions exist that require a complaint or sanction from a competent authority before a court can take cognizance, and these are generally not held to be unconstitutional.
